rationales: Ionization energy is the energy required to remove an electron, not the tendency to lose one.
Electropositivity is the tendency of an atom to lose valence electrons.
Valency is an atom's combining capacity.
Hardness describes resistance to scratching or deformation.
Graphite is relatively soft because its layers can slide over one another.
Phosphorus is not extremely hard.
Iodine is a relatively soft crystalline non-metal.
Diamond is extremely hard because of its strong covalent network structure.
H₂ is a diatomic molecule containing two atoms.
NH₃ is not diatomic; each molecule contains four atoms.
O₂ is a diatomic molecule containing two atoms.
HCl is a diatomic molecule containing two atoms.
An ionic bond forms through electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
A covalent bond generally involves a shared pair of electrons, but this is not the specific name for a dative bond.
A metallic bond involves attraction between metal ions and delocalized electrons.
A dative covalent bond is also called a coordinate covalent bond.
The O shell has five subshells, not three.
The N shell has four subshells, not three.
The L shell has two subshells, not three.
The M shell has three subshells: 3s, 3p, and 3d.
Mendeleev's postulate organized elements mainly by atomic mass, not the basis of the modern long-form table.
The long-form periodic table is constructed on the basis of atomic number.
Atomic mass is not the ordering basis of the modern long-form periodic table.
Valency is not the fundamental basis for arranging elements in the long-form table.
Fluorine has the highest electronegativity of the halogens.
Chlorine is less electronegative than fluorine.
Bromine is less electronegative than chlorine and fluorine.
Iodine is less electronegative than the other listed halogens.
Sodium has one electron in its outermost shell: its configuration is 2, 8, 1.
Sodium has one, not seven, valence electrons.
Eleven is sodium's total number of electrons in a neutral atom, not its valence-shell count.
Twenty-three is approximately sodium's mass number, not its valence-shell electron count.
Charles presented his law in 1787.
1662 is associated with Boyle's law, not Charles's law.
1913 is not the year Charles presented his law.
1932 is not the year Charles presented his law.
% m/m expresses grams of solute per 100 g of solution.
% m/v expresses grams of solute per 100 cm³ of solution.
% v/m expresses cm³ of solute per 100 g of solution.
% v/v expresses cm³ of solute per 100 cm³ of solution.
NaCl is a strong electrolyte that dissociates extensively in water.
NaOH is a strong electrolyte that dissociates extensively in water.
H₂SO₄ is generally classified as a strong electrolyte.
CH₃COOH is a weak electrolyte because it ionizes only partially in water.
Hydrogen has oxidation number −1 in metal hydrides.
Hydrogen is usually +1 in compounds with non-metals, not in metal hydrides.
Hydrogen does not have oxidation number −2 in metal hydrides.
Hydrogen does not have oxidation number +2 in metal hydrides.
Phosphorus is not ordinarily cited as a lustrous non-metal.
Graphite can have a sheen, but the standard textbook example of a lustrous non-metal is iodine.
Sulphur is generally dull rather than lustrous.
Iodine is the standard textbook example of a lustrous non-metal.
6.02 × 10²³ atoms is Avogadro's number, equivalent to 1 mole of carbon atoms.
Half a mole contains about 3.01 × 10²³ atoms.
0.2 mole contains about 1.20 × 10²³ atoms.
0.1 mole contains about 6.02 × 10²² atoms.
Helium has two electrons, unlike sodium's configuration after losing one electron.
After losing one electron, sodium has 10 electrons and the neon configuration.
Argon has 18 electrons, more than sodium has after losing one electron.
Xenon has 54 electrons, more than sodium has after losing one electron.
